The Board of Directors is pleased to present the strategic report for the year ended 31 December 2026.

Magnificent Cuisine Limited is a premium supplier of kitchens and related products to individual and corporate customers. We manufacture, retail and install kitchens, alongside offering kitchen design services, and retail kitchen appliances, cookware, kitchenware and tableware.

in sales of homeware, cookware and appliances from £301.9m to £263.2m. This reflects a shift in customer behaviour, with lower volumes of retail product purchases and significantly stronger demand for bespoke kitchen design, build and installation services, supported by increased installation activity and the Group’s growing presence in higher‑value, service‑led corporate and consumer contracts.

The Group delivered a strong trading performance in 2026, driven by continued demand for bespoke kitchen installations, improved operational efficiency, and the successful integration of newly acquired operations. Strategic developments during the year included the acquisition of Smith Kitchens Ltd, which has strengthened the Group’s manufacturing capacity and expanded its corporate customer offering.

The Group saw a 21% increase in profit in comparison with the prior year. The Group’s profit for the year was £52.1m (2025: £43.0m profit). Turnover was £545.3m (2025: £495.0m) — 10% higher than the prior year.

The Group remains focused on controlling overheads while continuing to manage cost pressures effectively. In 2026, global tariff volatility posed challenges for international supply chains and raw material sourcing. The Group responded proactively by diversifying its supplier base, and renegotiating key contracts to mitigate exposure to US-imposed tariffs on kitchen components and appliances. As a result, gross margin remained resilient, supported by improved sourcing strategies and a shift toward higher-margin, UK-manufactured premium products. Despite these efforts, fleet and transport costs remain high driven by increased freight charges, customs processing delays, and rerouting of shipments to avoid tariff-heavy corridors.

Operating profit for the year increased by £15.9m to a profit of £77.0m compared to last year (2025: £61.1m profit). Our adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation amortisation and impairment of non-financial assets increased by 29% from £72.5m to a profit of £93.3m as shown in the ‘alternative performance measures’ section below. The gross profit margin was 50% (2025: 46%) — 9% higher than the prior year.

The Group is not directly exposed to the geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East or Eastern Europe; however, indirect effects have been felt across global supply chains and energy markets. While the Group has not experienced any material disruption to its financial performance in 2026, it continues to monitor developments closely. Strategic contingency planning, including diversified logistics routes and supplier risk assessments, has helped mitigate potential exposure. Analysts remain cautious about the potential for future escalations and their impact on global trade flows, energy availability, and consumer sentiment.

The increase in revenue and profit compared to 2025 reflects the Group’s strong performance in an economy experiencing an uneven recovery despite ongoing global trade tensions. There was improved consumer confidence and spending following inflationary pressures easing in 2025. The Group benefited from a rebound in discretionary spending, particularly in home improvement, as households resumed investment in their homes rather than move house due to the high costs of moving. Revenue from kitchen design, build and installation services increased £88.9m from £193.1m to £282.0m this year. However, this was offset by a £38.7m decrease

The Group’s strong domestic market position and premium brand offering enabled it to absorb external pressures while continuing to deliver high-quality products and services to both individual and corporate customers.

The acquisition of Smith Kitchens Ltd for £7.7m represented a key strategic milestone during the year. This investment supports the Group’s objective of increasing its presence in the corporate house‑building sector. Post‑acquisition restructuring costs of £5.0m (2025: £Nil) were incurred to streamline manufacturing and warehousing facilities, resulting in redundancies.

There has been no change from the prior year to concentration of credit risk, and our experience of bad debts remains comparatively low. Stocks have also risen from £49.2m to £64.0m mainly due to the higher raw materials holdings as safety stock due to supply and shipping issues, together with a higher level of work in progress on bespoke kitchen installation contracts in line with the revised point‑in‑time revenue recognition policy. The Group spent £2.8m (2025: £0.4m) on research and development to support the development of new premium kitchen ranges, reflecting the Group’s ongoing commitment to product innovation.

The rise in current assets has been offset by a £27.3m uplift in current liabilities from £70.2m to £97.5m. This is mainly due to an increase of £8.6m in accruals as the Group have expanded the use of subcontractors leading to higher accruals for work performed but not invoiced, including in the acquired business. There has been an increase in lease liabilities of £3.0m from £1.3m to £4.3m due to the recognition of the obligations required under the revised Section 20 Leases of FRS 102, and a rise in corporation tax payable from £8.8m to £18.8m. Payments received on account have increased from £4m to £8.8m primarily due to the new customer contracts entered into during the year and the new point-in-time recognition policy.

During the year, the Group adopted the 2024 amendments to FRS 102. The amendments introduce revised requirements for revenue recognition and lease accounting. The transition has an insignificant impact on the Group’s financial performance for the year; the change from recognising revenue over time to recognising it at the point of customer acceptance under the revised Section 23 resulted in an increase of £3,383k in revenue and a £677k increase in profit. For lease accounting, it resulted in the recognition of right-of-use assets of £33.9m and additional lease liabilities of £27.7m on the balance sheet at 1 January 2026. The impact on the current period of applying the revised Section 20 is a decrease in profit of £643k. Further details are presented in note 2.29.

Depreciation, amortisation, and impairment of non-financial assets increased by £4.8m to £16.2m (2025: £11.4m). This was mainly due to the depreciation of the newly recognised right-of-use assets of £3.9m and impairment of software assets of £0.8m. The net asset position of the Group is £158.8m (2025: £96.9m).

Non-current liabilities have risen by £1.0m from £113.7m to £114.7m. £10m of bank loans were repaid in the year, but there was an increase in lease liabilities of £20.8m from £6.9m to £27.7m as a result of the amendments to Section 20 Leases of FRS 102. The other significant movement is in the net pension scheme liability which has decreased £8.9m from £55.0m to £46.1m mainly due to actuarial gains in the measurement of the liability offset by a negative return on assets due to poor performance in equity markets. The Group remains committed to ensuring that the pension fund deficit will be addressed over the coming years.

Investments have increased £2.3m from £3m to £5.3m due to the new joint venture formed on 29 December 2026. Magnificent Cuisine Limited formed Happy Kitchens Ltd with Solutions Ltd as their partner and both parties contributed £2.2m to the arrangement.

Current assets have increased from £179.2m to £239.9m, a rise of £60.7m. Of this, £35.5m relates to the growth in debtors derived from new contracts with customers entered into in the year with the increase reflecting the timing of invoicing and cash collection on recently completed installations and larger customer contracts. The customer experience is important to the Group. We want all of our customers to be delighted with all aspects of the products and service they receive from us. This relates to both retail kitchenware sales and to the actual kitchen sales from the moment they contact us, throughout the quotation process and the installation. All customers are sent on-line customer satisfaction surveys to voluntarily complete and certain customers depending on the value of the contract are invited to have an interview with our independent market researchers. All answers are scored between 1 to 5 with 1 being the lowest level and 5 being the highest level of customer satisfaction. The Group strives to get everything right but acknowledges that the scores given to such questions are subjective. To allow for this, the Board considers that a score of 3.5 and above is acceptable. All scores below this are investigated and subject to a root cause assessment to make sure that any lessons that should be learned are identified and implemented.

The Group’s strategy is to remain operating within the household goods sector for the medium to long term. However, in the shorter term the Group is looking to win more business with large corporate house building customers. Historically, the Group has focussed on exclusively serving individual consumers. Taking into account the capabilities that have been added through strategic acquisitions, the Board considers that the Group has the expertise to start to work with larger corporate customers as well as continuing to maintain the Group’s position as a premier supplier of kitchens and related products in its chosen markets.

The Group will not seek to win business at any price and will apply pricing strategies that reflect cost pressures while remaining mindful of household budgets. The move to working with large corporate house building customers should also help mitigate this risk.

Supply chain Again, the current global economic situation is impacting on the supply chain and our customers expect stock to be on hand.

The Group builds strong relationships with suppliers and for our significant raw material supplies, procurement teams review and renegotiate key supplier contracts periodically to ensure a diversified supplier base and the availability of key kitchen components and appliances. However, to avoid disruption in the current climate we have also increased our safety stock levels.
Integration of acquired business into the Group

The Group seeks to make acquisitions that complement its core business activities and that will contribute to the overall success of the Group for its stakeholders. However, there is a risk that the Group fails to achieve this objective on future acquisitions.

The Group undertakes a robust due diligence exercise on all potential acquisitions which involves the engagement of specialist external advisers as well as senior members of the Group’s management team. If there is any uncertainty as to the potential success of an acquisition, a full report is prepared for the Board to consider whether or not the transaction should proceed.
The Group operates in a competitive market environment and the development of new product ranges is key to our success.

Customer care is a top priority and the Group maintains strong relationships with customers. The Group provides value added services that enhance this loyalty as well as investing in innovation and design with new products launched every 3-years to meet evolving needs and differentiate our offerings.
Our section 172 statement summarises how the Board has factored stakeholder considerations into our decision-making.

The Group Directors believe strongly in doing business in the right way, with all its decisions underpinned by the impact they have on our five main stakeholder groups. We set out below two key areas where our Board had regard to Section 172 when discharging its duties and the effect of this on certain of its decisions.

Section 172 of the Companies Act 2006 (the Act) imposes a duty on a director to act in a way that he or she considers, in good faith, would be most likely to promote the long-term success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. In doing so, the directors have regard to the various matters including the interests of stakeholders as well as various other matters. The Companies (Miscellaneous Reporting) Regulations 2018 require companies to report on how the Board has fulfilled the requirements of Section 172(1), including how the Board has factored stakeholder considerations into its decision-making.

Remuneration policy: Having taken external advice on shareholder expectations, we revised our approach to executive remuneration by introducing a KPI aimed at our customer satisfaction ratings. Our customers represent one of our key stakeholder groups and we have therefore prioritised them in our executive director incentive measurements. In implementing the remuneration policy, we further considered the perceptions of our customers by setting our executive compensation far lower than our remuneration consultants recommended as it is our customers who ultimately pay for executive reward.
The Board is fully aware of and supports these requirements. We are pleased to describe below how the Group Board engages with our stakeholders.

The Group’s key stakeholders have an important role to play in the successful operation of our business. Our Board are fully aware of, and take seriously, their responsibilities to those stakeholders under the Act.

We believe that it is appropriate to consider the potential impact on our stakeholders when considering the Group’s strategy and in making our key decisions. Indeed, these responsibilities are rooted in our culture, values and company purpose.

Corporate responsibility (CR): Our employees are passionate about the societal, economic and environmental impact of the Group. During the past year, they took the initiative in developing their vision of what the Group’s CR was. The vision sets out our belief that our business has a positive impact on the world, offering a path to sustainability, carbon neutrality, equality and education – so directly affecting all our stakeholders. The Board will ensure that our employees’ vision of how the Group should conduct itself are considered when implementing CR policies.

The detailed content in this Annual Report further outlines how during 2026 the Board strove to comply with their duty under Section 172 in considering stakeholders in the Group’s decision-making process in order to promote the company’s success. We will continue to consider our stakeholders in the year ahead as the Board makes further decisions in overseeing the Group’s strategy. The following narrative summarises our approach.

The Board considers that, in its decisions and actions to date, it has acted in a way that would promote the success of the Group for the benefit of its members as a whole, while having regard to stakeholders and matters set out in Section 172(1) (a–f) of the Act. It has identified the Group’s key stakeholders as our employees, customers, suppliers and vendors, the environment and communities in which we operate, and investors. It receives updates on each of these and takes steps to ensure that it remains well informed about them.

We consider that our employees act with the utmost integrity and professional expertise in providing our customers with premium kitchens and related products. In doing so, the Board considers that its employees are both rewarded fairly and incentivised to deliver the Group’s strategy.
How we engage with our employees

The Board has put in place a structured governance model, with scheduled Board meetings and clear documentation and authority levels to control its decision-making process. Our governance model supports the Group in ensuring that decisions are considered, documented and reported upon, and in alignment with our strategic plans. Detailed budgets and reforecasts are prepared to enable the Board to track performance and ensure that it is as expected, or that mitigation steps are taken to deliver performance in line with, or close to, expectations. The Board and individual directors operate within this structure, with the aim of promoting the success of the company and delivering long-term shareholder value. Business proposals are documented in line with, and performance tracked against, levels of authority.

The Board is kept informed on employee-related matters at every Board meeting at which it receives a standing agenda update from the Group’s Human Resources Director. For our senior people, feedback is regularly received from the work that our remuneration committee undertakes throughout the year. Employee surveys are undertaken regularly to monitor issues arising and these surveys form the basis of action plans. Consultation with employees happens when their views need to be considered in decisions the Group needs to make that will likely affect their interests. All employees are kept abreast of Group news and financial performance in quarterly business updates. There is also ongoing communication through the Group’s Intranet, notice boards, newsletters and team briefings.
Our customer base is changing as we move into the large corporate house-builders market as well as selling to individual consumers.

We have a Code of Conduct setting out the behaviours and values expected of all of our colleagues, which we communicate to all colleagues and third parties. We have processes to update our Board and management on the operation of our code and an independent whistleblowing service to enable employees and third parties to anonymously raise concerns. Through its oversight and monitoring role, the Board requires all of our people to work to the highest standards of business conduct. Our focus is to do what is right ahead of what is easy. This is supported through ongoing communication and awareness of, and training in, acceptable company conduct. Any reports of inappropriate behaviour are independently investigated, and action taken where necessary.
We set out below how the Board has engaged with, and been influenced by, the interests of our different stakeholders. Such engagements have been well established in the Group for several years.

Our underlying business ethos is to do what is right ahead of what is easy. This is especially so when it comes to the local communities in which we operate and the impact that we have on the environment in which we all live. We actively encourage all of our employees to give back to community in whichever way they feel the most comfortable. This ranges from the ability to give to chosen charities via payroll deductions, matching donations that our employees have raised through their own endeavours subject to a cap or providing up to a week’s unpaid leave to volunteer in the community.

At each board meeting, as part of a standing agenda item, a report is received from the chief operating officer on any feedback received from customers from our interactions with them. This could be through regular key customer satisfaction surveys or simply from feedback received from our sales team. We take this information into account so that we are able to be confident that we have identified the appropriate customer needs that require addressing. From a risk management perspective, before entering into business with new customers full background checks are carried out which include reviews for potential financial risks.

We have built good relationships with our suppliers. Our raw materials, components and stock items are all carefully specified, and our suppliers are evaluated in accordance with our guidelines on the environment, work environment, human rights, business ethics and quality.
Other third parties that are of great importance to the Group include our professional advisers, bankers and our various regulators.

Our Board and our senior management colleagues are cognisant of the effect that our operations and those who provide us with goods and services have on the environment and seek to minimise our impact. Every three years, we consult with environmental consultants to ensure that our physical locations are as energy efficient as possible. Our last review was 18 months ago and following that we increased the cooling temperature setting used on air conditioning systems to reduce cost and environmental impact while at the same time providing optimal working conditions. We also work with our customers to provide a solution that enables redundant kitchens, that we are replacing, to be recycled in a safe and responsible manner. 65% of sales to customers resulted in redundant kitchens being safely removed for recycling or disposal as appropriate. This was an increase from 52% of such sales in the prior year reflecting both an increased awareness of our sales teams of the importance of minimising the impact on the environment as well as an increasing appreciation of the effects by our customers.

The Board is kept fully informed about the Group’s interactions with key third party relationships with the Group, be the suppliers or other key providers of services or regulatory oversight. The Board places the utmost importance on the integrity of our supplier agreements with a focus on the robustness of supply of goods and services. All third- party suppliers are regularly scrutinised so as to ensure that there are no matters that could potentially harm our reputation or be financially damaging to us. All agreements with third parties are set out in writing with clearly documented terms and conditions that cover, amongst other things, levels of service, payment terms and working practices. It is the Group’s policy that all agreements over a specified amount are reviewed by the Group’s lawyers and depending on the value are reserved for approval by the Board on behalf of the Group.

We have dispersed ownership and our investors are critical to us. They provide us with scarce risk capital that enables us to grow and invest for the future. However, our investors are not interested in growth at all costs. They take interest in our business plan, our strategy at to its execution, our governance, our approach to remuneration of both the Board and other members of the senior management team. Increasingly, they are becoming more interested in how we conduct ourselves as corporate citizens.
How we engage and what we do with that information

During the year, the Chair and the executive directors engage with shareholders at various events around the announcement of half-year and full-year results. From these engagement activities, the Board has a detailed understanding of the needs of our investors. This led to the development of the investor relations hub on the Group’s website that contains relevant and up to date information on the business. The Board is aware that it has a duty to treat all shareholders fairly and that it must ensure that all decisions made take the long-term interests of all shareholders into account.

This section of the Strategic report constitutes the Group’s non-financial and sustainability information statement to comply with the Companies (Strategic report) (Climate-related Financial Disclosure) Regulations 2022.

The Group Board is responsible for overseeing climate-related risks. Climate-related risks are embedded within the Group’s risk management framework, ensuring that our level of oversight and approach to identifying and monitoring them are consistent with the Group’s purpose, vision and strategy.

The Board’s assessment of risk is reflected both in the strategic decisions it takes and in the identification of Group principal risks and emerging risks, which have the ability to affect achievement of agreed strategic objectives and, in turn, long-term success.

The Board has created a Climate Risk Steering Group which is led by the Operations Director, who meets quarterly and feeds into the Board any climate-related issues through presentations across dedicated strategy sessions and within Board meetings, which cover the substance of the physical and transitional opportunities and risks associated with climate change. The Operations Director holds overall accountability for implementing climate-related initiatives in line with the agreed strategy and for driving progress against these commitments. As part of this responsibility, the Operations Director alongside the CFO set the Group’s annual objectives, which incorporate climate-related priorities and actions.
(b) Processes for identifying, assessing, and managing climate-related risks and opportunities, and their integration into the group’s overall risk management framework

Identification of climate-related risks is embedded within the Group’s risk management processes and forms part of the overall risk management framework. Our assessment approach considers both current and emerging risks. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for risk oversight, including climate-related risks, ensuring alignment with the Group’s strategic objectives.

During the year, our senior management team updated the Group’s risks and opportunities register including a scenario-based analysis to ensure it captured the impact of the evolving climate related risks on our business strategy, over relevant time horizons. The climate-related risks identified are consistently included in the register and the Climate Risk Steering Group reviews how the different climate-related risks might impact the company’s business model, including the potential for regulatory changes, shifts in consumer behaviours, or physical impacts due to climate change.

The Climate Risk Steering Group ensures that climate-related risks are identified, assessed, and integrated into the company’s broader risk management processes. This includes physical risks (like extreme weather events) and transition risks (such as changes in regulation, market, or technology).
(c) Principal risks, opportunities, and time horizons

The Group’s strategic roadmap has enabled the identification of climate-related risks and opportunities across three distinct time horizons, as outlined in the table below. Through continuous assessment and monitoring, we maintain a clear understanding of these risks and opportunities, allowing us to engage transparently with stakeholders and track progress effectively. This approach ensures we remain on course to achieve our climate-related objectives.
• Operational efficiency: Initiatives have been implemented to minimise energy consumption and reduce waste across our operations.
• Regulatory compliance: The Group is subject to increasingly stringent requirements relating to carbon emissions, energy efficiency, and product standards.
• Emerging market segments: Growing demand for sustainable products and services presents opportunities for expansion into new markets.
• Market risks: Variability in the cost of raw materials and energy, driven by climate-related policies, has the potential to affect profitability.
• Innovation: Continued investment in technologies that enhance climate resilience and support sustainable practice.
• Supply chain disruptions: Extreme weather events and other climate-related impacts may interrupt supply chain operations.
• Resilient supply chains: Enhancing supply chain resilience through diversification and localisation strategies, providing a competitive edge.
• Strategic partnerships: Collaborating on sustainability initiatives, including circular economy principles, to strengthen resilience and unlock new business models.
• Sustainable investments: Developing environmentally responsible products and services to meet the growing demand for green alternatives.
• Changing consumer preferences: Increasing awareness of climate issues could shift demand toward more sustainable products, affecting traditional offerings.
• Long-term market leadership: Ongoing investment in climate-resilient technologies and sustainable practices positions the Group to become a leader in an evolving market landscape.

• Physical risks: Long-term climate change impacts such as rising sea levels, prolonged droughts, and increased frequency of extreme weather events pose significant threats to operations, infrastructure, and potentially entire business models.
(d) Impacts on business model and strategy

The impact of climate-related risks and opportunities on the Group’s business model, strategy, and financial planning is multifaceted. As outlined in the table above these risks and opportunities directly influence our operations, competitive positioning, resources allocation and future planning. Climate considerations are integrated into strategic decision-making to ensure resilience and long- term value creation.
Physical risks, supply chain disruptions and operational resilience

Acute physical risks, such as extreme weather events (storms, floods, wildfires), and chronic risks, including rising sea levels and prolonged droughts, could disrupt supply chains and damage infrastructure across our global operations in the UK, France, Italy, USA, Colombia, and New Zealand. These disruptions may lead to delays in kitchen manufacturing and installation, increased logistics costs, and potential loss of revenue. These risks, which include both direct physical impacts and supply chain disruptions as identified in the table above, are mitigated through our strategy of diversifying suppliers, localising critical components, and investing in climate-resilient infrastructure to safeguard continuity of service and protect our premium brand reputation.
Regulatory compliance, changing consumer preferences and transition risks

Transition risks arising from stricter carbon regulations, energy efficiency standards, and evolving consumer preferences toward sustainable products may require significant changes to our product design, material sourcing, and manufacturing processes. These changes could increase compliance costs and affect profitability if not addressed proactively. Conversely, they present opportunities to innovate and expand our range of eco-friendly kitchens, energy-efficient appliances, and sustainable materials. Our strategic roadmap prioritises sustainability-led innovation and adaptation to regulatory requirements and consumer trends, ensuring compliance and maintaining premium positioning in a transforming market.
Market risks, financial performance and growth opportunities

Climate-related policies and market dynamics may influence raw material and energy costs, impacting margins and pricing strategies. At the same time, opportunities exist to capture new market segments and build strategic partnerships focused on circular economy principles. These market risks, particularly variability in input costs, are addressed by embedding climate considerations into our investment planning, focusing on operational efficiency, cost reduction, and long-term growth through sustainable product development and resilient supply chains. Continued investment in climate-resilient technologies and sustainable practices position the Group to mitigate market risks and capitalise on opportunities, supporting our ambition to emerge as a market leader in a transformed global landscape.

The Group has assessed the resilience of its business model and strategy against a range of plausible climate-related scenarios to understand potential impacts and inform long-term planning. This analysis considers both physical risks (acute and chronic) and transition risks across our global operations and supply chain.
We selected scenarios aligned with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) pathways and the Paris Agreement targets, reflecting a range of potential global temperature outcomes:

High transition risk: regulatory compliance costs, product redesign, supply chain adaptation.
Rapid transition to a low- carbon economy with accelerated emissions reductions and stricter regulations.
Invest in sustainable materials and energy- efficient appliances; embed sustainability in product innovation; enhance operational efficiency.
2°C Stabilisation Moderate transition with progressive regulatory changes and market adaptation.
Balanced transition and physical risks: gradual compliance requirements, moderate supply chain disruption.

• Mitigation measures: Supplier diversification, localisation of key operations, investment in sustainable technologies, and integration of climate considerations into capital planning.

• Assumptions: Analysis is qualitative, based on IPCC scenarios and Paris Agreement targets. Assumes progressive regulatory tightening under 1.5°C and 2°C scenarios and increased frequency of extreme weather under 3.5°C scenario.
• Residual risks: Despite mitigation, physical risks under high-warming scenarios may lead to increased costs and operational complexity.

• Business review: section 414C requires entities to present a fair and balanced review of their businesses consistent with their size and complexity. This includes development and performance of the business of the entity (or group) during the financial year, and the position of the entity (or group) at year-end. To the extent necessary, financial and non-financial KPIs should be used to explain further the performance or position of the entity (or group). In applying these requirements, it is typically appropriate to include commentary on the key line items and sub-totals in the primary statements in the accounts. If non-GAAP measures of financial performance and position are used (sometimes referred to as ‘Alternative Performance Measures‘ or ‘APMs’), then equivalent GAAP numbers should generally be disclosed with equal prominence and reconciliations between the GAAP and non-GAAP figures provided.

The business review should also include a description of the principal risks and uncertainties facing the entity. This section should clearly state the principal risks and describe them in a way to enable users to understand the nature of the risk or uncertainty and how it might affect the entity. It should also state why they are important, what their effect is and what procedures, or controls have been implemented by the board to manage them.

• Section 172 Statement: this statement is applicable to large private entities and all public companies regardless of their size. It should be presented as a distinct statement within the strategic report and should be specific to the entity (or group). It should aim to provide shareholders with meaningful, transparent information on how the directors have performed their s172 duty and had regard to wider stakeholder interests. It should explain how the directors have duly considered the six areas outlined in s172(1)(a)-(f) while promoting the success of the entity. This explanation should typically cover the main methods used to engage with stakeholders, key issues identified and how these have influenced the board’s decisions, plans and strategies over the course of the year.

Judgment is needed in determining what should be included in the statement as this will depend on the nature of the entity, its business, ownership structure and developments in the year, among other factors. The length and contents of these statements therefore vary but a statement that simply confirms that s172 has been followed, or a general explanation of governance procedures is unlikely to be sufficient to fulfil this legal obligation.

Revenue from the sale of goods and services to customers is recognised by applying the five-step model, which is designed to represent the transfer of promised goods or services to customers. The amount recognised reflects the consideration the company expects to be entitled to in exchange for those goods or services.

The company sells cookware, kitchenware, tableware, kitchen appliances, and kitchen units. Customers purchase these goods directly from the Group’s retail stores or website. Goods can be delivered for an extra charge.

The performance obligation is satisfied when control of the specific good has been transferred to the customer which is the point in time the customer takes physical possession of the goods. This is either the point where the customer takes the purchased goods from the store or the point at which the goods are delivered to the customer’s chosen location.

Payment is due at the point of sale, unless a customer opts to finance their purchase (subject to appropriate credit checks), which may grant a period of up to 3 months’ interest-free credit. However, as the maximum period of finance offered is less than 12 months, the Group applies the practical expedient and does not adjust for the time value of money.

Payment received for goods which have not yet been delivered are recognised as payments received on account, until control passes to a customer on delivery of the goods. At this point, the payment received on account is derecognised, and revenue is recognised. The lead time between purchase and delivery is short and is usually a period of 3 to 5 business days.

All goods are subject to the Group’s returns policy which allows the customer the right to return the purchased good in return for a full refund, store credit or product exchange within 28 days of original purchase, provided the goods are in working order and have their original undamaged packaging. Revenue from the sale of goods is constrained based on the best estimate of expected levels of goods to be returned by customers. In addition, a refund asset (as a component of stocks) is recognised representing the expected carrying amount of products expected to be returned, as well as a refund liability (as a component of creditors) which represents the expected consideration to be refunded to customers. The refund asset and refund liability are remeasured each reporting period, with corresponding adjustments to the costs of sales and revenue respectively. The policy does not apply to instances where a customer exchanges one product for another of the same type, quality, condition and price.

Goods are sold with a standard assurance-type warranty, which does not constitute a separate performance obligation. The warranty merely assures that products meet agreed-upon specifications; therefore, revenue is recognised in full when control is transferred to the customer.

Provision of design, build & installation services

In addition to the sale of goods, the Group offers bespoke kitchen design and build services tailored to individual customer specifications. These services include the design, construction, and installation of custom kitchens for customers.

The Group offers customers high-end bespoke kitchen designs and quotations at no charge. If the customer does not proceed, the company retains control of the design. The design element is not a contractual promise, as control of the design remains with the Group until the customer accepts both the design and quote, initiating the build stage. Design and quote costs are expensed immediately since they would occur regardless of acceptance, and any potential asset’s amortisation period is less than one year.

The customer is quoted a single price for the package which includes design, build and installation services. The design, build and installation of high-end bespoke customer kitchens is accounted for as a single performance obligation as the individual elements are incapable of being distinct and are not separately identifiable. Appliances are separately quoted based on what the customers choose, and a customer is able to acquire the appliances from third party providers. Revenue from sale of appliances included within these types of contracts are treated as a separate performance obligation recognised in accordance with the policy for sale of goods above. Each element of the performance obligation is performed by the Group’s own highly skilled and trained designers, builders and installers.

Revenue for the design, build and installation of bespoke kitchens is recognised at a point in time and not over time because the Group does not have an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date, and, as the Group retains legal title over the kitchen cabinets and other bespoke components until the point of customer acceptance, the customer does not control the asset as it is created.

A non-refundable upfront deposit of 50% of the total contract value is billed upon acceptance of the design and quotation, and the remaining 50% billed upon completion. In the event of termination, the Group is only entitled to recover costs incurred to date not already covered by the initial non- refundable deposit. Therefore, the Group does not have the right to recover costs incurred plus a reasonable margin at all points over the duration of the contract. Payment for the remaining 50% of the contract value related to design, build & installation service is due 28 days after the completion of installation (dependent on customer acceptance being obtained), unless a customer opts to finance their purchase, where they may receive interest-free credit for a period of up to 9 months. However, as the maximum period of finance offered is less than 12 months, the Group applies the practical expedient and does not adjust for the time value of money.

Customer acceptance after installation confirms their control over the installed kitchen, as they can direct its use and benefit from it. Control transfers at the point of customer acceptance, which must occur within 24 hours of practical completion, which is the point at which revenue is recognised. Appliance installation is excluded, as customers may install these themselves or with third parties only after accepting the kitchen unit; this ensures the Group can address any issues if the kitchen does not meet specifications.

The Group also provides customers with a 10-year warranty in connection with the bespoke installed kitchen units. These types of warranties cannot be separately purchased by a customer. The warranties are only intended to safeguard customers against workmanship defects and do not provide any incremental services to a customer. For these reasons, warranties are not considered to be a separate performance obligation.
At the point of customer acceptance, the payment received on account is recognised as revenue and the remaining 50% of the transaction price outstanding is recognised as a trade receivable.

The following judgements had a significant effect on the amounts recognised in the financial statements:
Classification of corporate building as tangible fixed asset

The Group has entered into a short-term arrangement to lease space in its corporate building to third parties that is temporarily surplus to the Group’s own requirements. The lease is classified as an operating lease. Management has considered the requirements in FRS 102 to separate mixed-use property between investment property and property, plant and equipment if the resulting portions could be sold separately or leased out separately under a finance lease. Management has applied judgement to conclude that the nature of the leased portion, which comprises sections of different floors amounting to less than 10% of the entire building, does not meet the criteria for separation. The entire property is therefore accounted for as property, plant, and equipment.
The corporate building along with all freehold property is accounted for under the revaluation method and the fair value is estimated on annual basis (refer below for estimation uncertainty).
Significant judgements relating to the adoption of revised Section 23 – Revenue from contracts with customers, applicable from 1 January 2026.
Design, build and installation of bespoke customer kitchens

The design phase for bespoke customer kitchens is regarded as a pre-contract activity, as it takes place prior to the establishment of a binding contract. At this stage, the customer is not obliged to accept the proposed design and quotation, nor do they obtain control over the design itself. The contract is only considered to be approved, and the enforceable rights and obligations of both parties are identified, once the customer accepts both the design and the quotation. It is at this point that the obligations relating to the goods and services to be provided, namely the build and installation of the bespoke kitchen, become binding and enforceable.

In assessing the performance obligations, it is necessary to determine whether the build and installation services are (a) capable of being distinct, and (b) separately identifiable within the context of the contract. The build and installation services offered by the Group involve highly bespoke and specialised kitchen units, which require the expertise of trained professionals and often necessitate on-site adjustments to accommodate the specific measurements and conditions of each customer’s kitchen space. The Group does not sell the build and installation services separately, and customers can only purchase these services as part of a bundled package. The customer cannot benefit from the build service in isolation, as there are no other readily available resources, such as installation, which the customer can obtain elsewhere, or which have already been provided by the Group. Furthermore, the bespoke nature of the build and installation services means that they are highly interrelated and interdependent. Consequently, these combined services are accounted for as a single performance obligation, as they do not meet the criteria to be considered individually as distinct goods or services or as a series of substantially similar goods or services with the same pattern of transfer to the customer.
3. Judgements in applying accounting policies and key sources of estimation uncertainty (continued)
Appliances as a separate performance obligation

While appliances may, in many cases, be included within a customer’s design and quotation at their request, customers retain the freedom to source appliances and arrange for their installation through third-party suppliers. The installation of appliances is relatively straightforward, given that appliances are generally manufactured to standard dimensions, regardless of brand. Customers are thus able to benefit from appliances in conjunction with readily available resources — specifically, the previously installed kitchen units. The Group does not provide a significant service of integrating the appliances with the units, and neither the units nor the appliances are substantially modified or customised by being combined. Furthermore, there is no significant interrelation or interdependence between the kitchen units and the appliances. As a result, the transfer of appliances in contracts for bespoke kitchen installations is accounted for as a separate performance obligation.
Revenue recognition at point in time

Contracts for bespoke kitchen installations require a 50% non-refundable deposit upon design and quote acceptance, with the remaining 50% due 28 days after installation acceptance. Customers can terminate contracts but must pay costs incurred to date; while there is no alternative use to the entity for physical goods in process of manufacture and installation, under the terms of the contract the group retains legal title and has the right to remove the goods if termination occurs before customer acceptance. Since control of all work in progress is retained by the Group and another entity would need to start over, customers have no rights to unfinished assets. Though the bespoke units have no alternative use, the Group is only entitled to recover costs beyond the deposit upon early termination, and therefore does not have a right to recover costs plus a reasonable margin at all times during the contract. Therefore, revenue is recognised when the customer accepts the final installed kitchen, as the criteria for recognising revenue over time is not met.

The Group is exposed to various risks in relation to financial instruments. The Group’s financial assets and liabilities by category are summarised in note 22. The Group has exposures to three main areas of risk - foreign exchange currency exposure, liquidity risk and customer credit exposure. To a lesser extent the Group is exposed to interest rate risk.

The Group’s risk management is coordinated at its headquarters, in close cooperation with the board of directors, and focuses on actively securing the Group’s short to medium-term cash flows by minimising the exposure to volatile financial markets. The Group does not actively engage in the trading of financial assets for speculative purposes, nor does it write options.
The Group enters into derivatives, principally for hedging foreign exchange risk, however, hedge accounting is not applied.
The most significant financial risks to which the Group is exposed are described below.

The Group is exposed to currency exchange rate risk due to a significant proportion of its trade receivables, and trade payables for purchases of inventories, being denominated in non-sterling currencies.
The net exposure of each currency is monitored and managed by the use of forward foreign exchange contracts or overdrafts. The forward foreign exchange contracts all mature within 12 to 18 months.

The objective of the Group in managing liquidity risk is to ensure that it can meet its financial obligations as and when they fall due. The Group expects to meet its financial obligations through operating cash flows. In the event that the operating cash flows would not cover all the financial obligations the Group has credit facilities available.
Given the maturity of the bank loan in note 22.1, the Group is in position to meet its commitments and obligations as they come due.

The Group may offer credit terms to its customers which allow payment of the debt after delivery of the goods or services. The Group is at risk to the extent that a customer may be unable to pay the debt on the specified due date. This risk is mitigated by the strong on-going customer relationships and by credit insurance.

The Group borrows from its bankers using either overdrafts or term loans whose tenure depends on the nature of the asset and management’s view of the future direction of interest rates (see bank loans in note 22.1).

The dilapidation provision relates to estimated costs of rectification that the Group is liable for under the terms of the leases of its rented retail stores. Costs relating to the removal of leasehold improvements are included in the cost of the asset whilst costs relating to wear and tear are included in profit or loss.
